The Tahoe sucker Catostomus tahoensis is a large-bodied catostomid endemic to the Lake Tahoe Basin and adjacent drainages of the western Great Basin. Field surveys of adult individuals from the Truckee River system indicate that the species attains a maximum recorded total length of 61 centimeters [Li = 61 centimeters], a size that distinguishes it from smaller-bodied congeners that rarely exceed 40 centimeters in total length. The neonatal wet weight at birth, derived directly from the mean diameter of 1.8 millimeters observed in demersal eggs, is approximately 0.0031 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0031 grams], a minuscule initial mass that reflects the energetic constraints of yolk-dependent oogenesis in a cold-water environment. This species exhibits a pronounced shift in body mass over ontogeny; recently collected specimens demonstrate that the ultimate wet weight for adults reaches 2,680 grams [Wwi = 2,680 grams], representing a mass increase of nearly six orders of magnitude from the egg stage. The length-mass relationship reported for this stock follows a power-law exponent of approximately 3.04, consistent with isometric scaling patterns observed in other iteroparous freshwater teleosts.

Reproductive maturation in Tahoe sucker occurs at a relatively modest size compared to the species terminal dimensions. Examination of gonad recrudescence and histological staging of gametogenesis in a sample from Lake Tahoe revealed that total length at puberty is 14.5 centimeters [Lp = 14.5 centimeters], a threshold that typically corresponds to an age of four to five years based on scale annulus readings. The accompanying wet weight at puberty, predicted from the length-mass relationship applicable to this population, is 33.2 grams [Wwp = 33.2 grams]. The onset of vitellogenesis and spermiation at this size suggests that the transition from somatic growth to reproductive investment occurs well before the attainment of maximum body size, a pattern common among iteroparous riverine cypriniforms. The gonadosomatic index of pubertal individuals increases sharply at this length, confirming that 14.5 centimeters [Lp = 14.5 centimeters] represents a biologically meaningful developmental threshold rather than a statistical artifact of the length-frequency distribution.

Longevity records for Catostomus tahoensis, assembled from mark-recapture studies and validated otolith microchemistry analyses, indicate that the maximum lifespan in the wild reaches approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years] under the thermal regime characteristic of the Lake Tahoe Basin, where mean annual water temperature is 14 °C [T = 14 °C]. The corresponding total lived period of roughly 5,475 days [am = roughly 5,475 days] at this temperature places the species among the longer-lived members of the Catostomidae, a family in which maximum ages typically range from 8 to 20 years depending on latitude and thermal at a temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C] habitat. The slow pace of senescence inferred from this extreme longevity is likely linked to the low metabolic demand associated with cold-water residency; reports for other catostomids from similar thermal environments suggest that lifespan increases by roughly a month for each degree Celsius decline in mean habitat temperature. The 14 °C [T = 14 °C] thermal context of the Lake Tahoe population thus appears to facilitate a decelerated life history relative to conspecifics inhabiting warmer, lower-elevation streams.

The reproductive ecology of Tahoe sucker is characterized by a single annual spawning event in the spring, coinciding with peak snowmelt discharge. Gravid females produce between 1,200 and 3,600 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = between 1,200 and 3,600 eggs per spawning event], with clutch size positively correlated with maternal total length. The species exhibits a strict annual frequency of a single spawning event each year [F_R_i = single spawning event each year], driven by the pronounced seasonality of its native lacustrine and riverine environments. This annual reproductive schedule contrasts with that of some southern catostomids that spawn multiple times within a single warm season. The adhesive, demersal eggs are deposited over gravel-cobble substrates in shallow littoral zones, where incubation proceeds for approximately 8 to 12 days depending on water temperature. The combination of moderate fecundity and a single annual reproductive event yields a comparatively low daily reproductive output, a life-history strategy that prioritizes offspring survival in a stable, resource-predictable environment.

Comparative life-history analysis across catostomid species reveals that the Tahoe sucker occupies a moderate position on the slow-fast continuum of teleost life histories. Its ultimate total length of 61 centimeters [Li = 61 centimeters] is intermediate between the smaller, short-lived mountain sucker Catostomus platyrhynchus and the larger, long-lived June sucker Chasmistes liorus. The wet weight at birth of 0.0031 grams [Wwb = 0.0031 grams] is typical for a demersal-egg-producing catostomid of this adult size, and the 2,680 gram [Wwi = 2,680 gram] maximum body mass aligns with predictions from the general length-weight regression for the genus. The life cycle, framed by a 15-year maximum longevity (15 years) [am = 15 years] at 14 °C [T = 14 °C], demonstrates a decelerated pace that supports iteroparity and multiple spawning events across the adult lifespan. This combination of moderate size, delayed maturation, and extended lifespan distinguishes the Tahoe sucker from many cypriniform fishes that exhibit early maturity and semelparity in warmer, less stable habitats.
